title: Envy, softened
hookLine: mudita's far enemy is envy; its near enemy is giddy excitement

lines: A STORY TO MAKE IT HURT LESS.
cards: Envy may be the hardest feeling to own up to. People say they're angry, sad, tired, anxious. Fewer say, out loud, I'm envious of my sister.
It shows up anyway: scrolling past a colleague's promotion, a neighbor's new kitchen, a friend's easy-looking marriage.
It tightens something, and then comes a little story to make it hurt less: they got lucky, it won't last, it's not really that great.

teach.h: FAR ENEMY: ARATI, AND ISSA, ENVY.
teach.b: The Visuddhimagga's own name for mudita's far enemy is arati, aversion or discontent, the sour, fed-up feeling about someone else's good fortune.
It says mudita's job is to be unenvious, so some modern teachers simply call the far enemy envy, the Pali issa. They're close cousins: envy is discontent with a target.
It's the far enemy because it's the plain opposite of rejoicing.
Where mudita says, how wonderful for you, envy says, why you and not me?
The near enemy is subtler. The manual calls it joy based on the worldly life, a kind of excitement. Giddy excitement looks like mudita from the outside: exclamation points, big reactions.
But it's often about me: the thrill of the party, of being close to someone's success, of the gossip about it. It's bubbly, it fades quickly, and sometimes it curdles into envy the next morning.
Real mudita is steadier and quieter. It stays glad even when you're not in the photo. So how does envy soften?
The manual's advice is the same gentle order as with every room. Start with someone easy to be glad for, and let the gladness grow strong. Then turn it, a little at a time, toward someone harder.
And underneath sits a simple fact: someone else's happiness doesn't use up the world's supply. Their promotion isn't taken from your drawer.
When that lands, even briefly, envy has less to hold on to, and what was a tight fist can open into joy.

how: Meditation teachers present envy and excited, self-centered joy as the far and near enemies of mudita, and guide students to rejoice first for easy people and then, gradually, for people they envy.

o: the guilt that follows a selfish choice
discontent at someone else's good fortune
a healthy drive to match what others achieve

s: the manual's own word for mudita's far enemy is arati, discontent
some modern teachers call it envy, since mudita's job is to be unenvious.
loud excitement about someone's news is always mudita
it can be the near enemy: bubbly, about me, and quick to fade.
the manual says to start with the person you envy most
start with someone easy to be glad for, then turn toward harder people.

games.q: your colleague gets the promotion you wanted. envy flickers. what does today's teaching suggest?
o: tell yourself they just got lucky.
name the envy kindly, then offer one sincere word of gladness.
throw a huge party for them to prove you're fine.
games.why: envy softens slowly, by noticing it and turning gladness toward the person; the big party may be the near enemy, excitement that's really about you.

practice: Warm up with someone easy to be glad for, then gently bring to mind one person you envy a little, not the hardest one, and notice the tightening without scolding it.
Picture their good fortune making their day better, just as your good days make yours better. Then offer one breath of the wish, may your good fortune last; if it's stiff, that's all right.

wordCard.voice: Envy. Mudita's far enemy, the plain opposite of rejoicing; its near enemy is giddy excitement that's really about me.

orig.note: Pali issā: envy; the manual names mudita's far enemy arati (discontent), which some modern teachers call envy.
